sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Cleft sentences
sources.conclusion: Cleft splits one message into a focus and an understood clause. Human focus permits who or that; what-cleft identifies focused information after be. The page also illustrates a bare infinitive following a what-clause containing need to do. Do not infer that every wh-initial subject clause is the same focused construction, or that infinitives are prohibited after be.
sources.not_claimed: Full body direct access; a published exact What I need is to rest example.

sources.title: British Council — Emphasis: cleft sentences, inversion and auxiliaries
sources.conclusion: The editorial body covers focus-preserving it-clefts, spoken what-clefts, fronted negative adverbial inversion, and stressed auxiliaries/do in speech and writing. It uses a broader wh-cleft label including a how-clause with an unclear predicate; retain this terminological breadth explicitly rather than declaring all such clauses ungrammatical.
sources.limit: This is a C1-labelled reference; M84 own practice remains a controlled B2 focus, not a claim that all negative inversion is basic B2.

sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Inversion
sources.conclusion: Fronted negative adverbials trigger auxiliary/modal-before-subject order in the relevant emphatic construction. The unchanged neutral order with noninitial never remains grammatical. Existing tense and lexical verb are retained; do-support is used only where the model requires it.

sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Not only … but also
sources.conclusion: Clause-fronted not only can trigger inversion; ordinary internal not only does not. The source's unconditional after Not only rule must be narrowed by syntactic scope; a subject list beginning Not only Tom but also Lea has its ordinary subject before the verb.

sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Fronting
sources.conclusion: Fronting changes focus, not necessarily subject-verb order. Literary locative/directional inversion with a noun phrase must not become a universal pronoun permutation. Object fronting can also occur in speech, so formal-only labels are too strong.

sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Personal pronouns
sources.conclusion: Object forms occur as complements of be; subject forms such as It is I are more formal. Applied to the source's she/her cleft example, present both accepted registers without a she-only rule. This application is an editorial inference from the copular-complement rule, not an exact quoted cleft pair.

sources.title: Cambridge Dictionary — To, infinitive use
sources.conclusion: A to-infinitival clause can occupy a copular complement, and need licenses to-infinitives. Combined with the focus construction in E-cleft, What I need is to rest is a valid focused action reading. This is a composition of two attested rules, explicitly an inference, not a publisher exercise answer.

sources.title: Cambridge Dictionary — Need
sources.conclusion: Lexical need licenses a noun complement and a to-infinitive. Some rest and to rest are both well-formed ways to express a need; a single-key grammaticality task cannot oppose them as correct/incorrect.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: Clause patterns depend on the verb; transitive and intransitive uses differ, and objects/complements/adverbials are not one interchangeable slot.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: A SVO is the neutral transitive model, not a mandatory object for every sentence. Subject need not be a physical doer; a complement after linking be is not an object.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: Ordinary adverbials follow verb or its object/complement; frequency normally precedes the lexical verb. Initial adverbials and pre-verbal manner are also possible.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: Do not label every initial time phrase or every changed order universally ungrammatical. Require the target neutral/end-time pattern visibly where only one order is keyed.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: One-word frequency adverbials usually precede the main verb but follow main be; every-phrases describe frequency too.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: Retain source frequency examples and qualify hero/summary with usually. Keep every morning as a time/frequency phrase, not a one-word adverb.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: Adverbials can occur front/mid/end. Frequency usually mid but can be front/end; manner-place-time is a normal preference, not universal grammar law. An ordinary short object is not split from its verb by the adverb.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: A every-day/go-to-school and every-week/supermarket corrections become explicit neutral-pattern tasks, not universal impossibility statements. Often input is explicitly restricted to before reads; every-morning input accepts both natural initial and final time order.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: SVO is typical in declaratives, but fronting can rearrange objects/complements/adjuncts for focus while preserving the message.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: Do not conflate marked/contextual order with grammatical impossibility; A tests neutral form only where the visible criterion says so.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: Some verbs have no object; linking verbs take subject complements rather than objects.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: A forms-grid distinguishes books after reads from a state after be; subject definition does not demand an action.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: Question inversion concerns the relevant first verb/auxiliary; Present/Past Simple lexical verbs use do/does/did and base form; subject questions retain subject-verb order, including Who is knocking.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: B retain ready, coming, swim and finished under correct be/modal/auxiliary-have categories. Do not invert the whole verb phrase or invent a lexical verb after ready.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: Yes/no questions place the first verb element before subject; negatives put not after the first auxiliary; do-support applies to relevant simple lexical-verb constructions.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: B preserve auxiliary chain and tense. Does/did consume the tense/agreement feature; retain play/watch/go base forms in transformations.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: Neutral simple-positive subject questions normally omit do, but emphatic subject questions can use do and negative subject questions require do when no other auxiliary is present. Perfect/Continuous questions can retain their own auxiliaries.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: B no-aux claim narrowed to no added do/does/did in the stated positive simple model. Short visible scope note keeps exceptions available without replacing A1 tasks by advanced drills.

primary_editorial_sources.finding: Declaratives can function as yes/no questions in spoken contexts, notably checking or surprise.
primary_editorial_sources.decision: B You like coffee? is not globally banned; the select explicitly asks for a neutral full interrogative with the appropriate auxiliary. Intonation is not assessed by the unchanged engine.

primary_editorial_sources.access: direct editorial body read, lines 1-33; comments excluded
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Звичайні кінцеві обставини йдуть після дієслова або його додатка/комплемента. Початкова обставина й прислівник способу перед основним дієсловом також можливі. Рекомендований нейтральний порядок не дорівнює універсальній забороні інших позицій.

primary_editorial_sources.access: direct canonical fetch returned 403; indexed primary editorial text read, not full direct-page access
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Для mid-position при кількох дієсловах орієнтир — після першого auxiliary/modal; copular be має іншу нейтральну позицію. Manner/place/time — типовий, не безвинятковий порядок. Here/there мають різний порядок із noun і pronoun subjects.

primary_editorial_sources.access: indexed primary editorial dialogue read; learner comments not used
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Окремі frequency adverbs допускають front/end; always і never не можна механічно переносити за тим самим правилом. Not always не означає never.
Adverb — клас слова; його функції не обмежені модифікацією дієслова. Група at home виконує обставинну функцію, але не стає одним adverb.

primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Місце передають і прийменникові групи; at home/in the park слід пояснювати як групи, а не перелік однословних прислівників.

primary_editorial_sources.access: direct canonical fetch returned 403; indexed primary editorial text read
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Much/very much не мають універсальної єдиної кінцевої позиції. У цільовому I like it very much група йде після object; це не забороняє формальне very much перед відповідним дієсловом або much у comparative.

primary_editorial_sources.access: direct editorial body read, lines 22-68; comments excluded
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Винесене на початок заперечне never для акценту потребує auxiliary-subject inversion. У нейтральному I have never... такого винесення немає; правило не запускається після будь-якого never. Старе завдання може перевіряти це як контрольоване поглиблення, не замінюючи A2-практику.

primary_editorial_sources.access: direct editorial body read, lines 22-84; exercise banks and comments not copied
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: У розділюваній transitive-моделі noun object має два порядки, pronoun object — між verb/particle. Нерозділювані конструкції та неперехідні значення не підлягають цьому правилу. Довгий object може мати іншу стилістичну перевагу.

primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Prepositional verbs на кшталт look after не розділяються. Фактичні phrasal-prepositional моделі put up with/look forward to мають verb+particle+preposition, але сама кількість написаних слів не є загальним алгоритмом розділюваності.

primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Для навчального узагальненого phrasal verb допустиме пояснення різних multiword моделей, але треба зберегти відмінність розділюваного particle verb та нерозділюваного prepositional verb. Це узгоджується з прийнятим M78.

primary_editorial_sources.access: direct canonical fetch returned 403; indexed primary editorial text read
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Після core modal наступне дієслово має base form; ним може бути auxiliary have/be. Semi-modal ought to та lexical/semi-modal have to не підпадають під blanket-заборону to.
Be/do/have бувають допоміжними й основними за конструкцією. Linking be не вимагає object; неперехідне дієслово теж може утворювати повне речення без object.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Cleft sentences
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Cleft splits one message into a focus and an understood clause. Human focus permits who or that; what-cleft identifies focused information after be. The page also illustrates a bare infinitive following a what-clause containing need to do. Do not infer that every wh-initial subject clause is the same focused construction, or that infinitives are prohibited after be.
primary_editorial_sources.not_claimed: Full body direct access; a published exact What I need is to rest example.

primary_editorial_sources.title: British Council — Emphasis: cleft sentences, inversion and auxiliaries
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: The editorial body covers focus-preserving it-clefts, spoken what-clefts, fronted negative adverbial inversion, and stressed auxiliaries/do in speech and writing. It uses a broader wh-cleft label including a how-clause with an unclear predicate; retain this terminological breadth explicitly rather than declaring all such clauses ungrammatical.
primary_editorial_sources.limit: This is a C1-labelled reference; M84 own practice remains a controlled B2 focus, not a claim that all negative inversion is basic B2.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Inversion
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Fronted negative adverbials trigger auxiliary/modal-before-subject order in the relevant emphatic construction. The unchanged neutral order with noninitial never remains grammatical. Existing tense and lexical verb are retained; do-support is used only where the model requires it.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Not only … but also
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Clause-fronted not only can trigger inversion; ordinary internal not only does not. The source's unconditional after Not only rule must be narrowed by syntactic scope; a subject list beginning Not only Tom but also Lea has its ordinary subject before the verb.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Fronting
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Fronting changes focus, not necessarily subject-verb order. Literary locative/directional inversion with a noun phrase must not become a universal pronoun permutation. Object fronting can also occur in speech, so formal-only labels are too strong.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Personal pronouns
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Object forms occur as complements of be; subject forms such as It is I are more formal. Applied to the source's she/her cleft example, present both accepted registers without a she-only rule. This application is an editorial inference from the copular-complement rule, not an exact quoted cleft pair.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Cambridge Dictionary — To, infinitive use
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: A to-infinitival clause can occupy a copular complement, and need licenses to-infinitives. Combined with the focus construction in E-cleft, What I need is to rest is a valid focused action reading. This is a composition of two attested rules, explicitly an inference, not a publisher exercise answer.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Cambridge Dictionary — Need
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Lexical need licenses a noun complement and a to-infinitive. Some rest and to rest are both well-formed ways to express a need; a single-key grammaticality task cannot oppose them as correct/incorrect.

primary_editorial_sources.title: British Council LearnEnglish Kids — Have got
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: The model covers belongings, family, and body characteristics. Have/has agrees with the subject; not follows have/has; question inversion uses have/has. Contractions are grammatical. Short answers repeat have/has and need no got.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Have got and have
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: In possession, relationships, and characteristics, have and have got can express the same state. Lexical-have questions with do are grammatical; do plus have got is not the target model. Do not extend this equivalence indiscriminately to meals, activities, obligation, or past get events.

metadata.prospective_learning_resource_descriptio: У нейтральному ствердному реченні зазвичай спочатку називаємо підмет, а потім дію чи стан. Додаток потрібний не кожному дієслову. Далі розглянемо частотність і місце обставин: інший порядок може бути допустимим, але мати інший акцент.

metadata.prospective_learning_resource_descriptio: У нейтральному повному питанні обирай потрібну форму do/does/did, be, модального або вже наявного допоміжного дієслова. У запереченні знайди місце not. Не переставляй усю дієслівну групу й не змінюй час або учасників повідомлення.

metadata.prospective_learning_resource_descriptio: Прислівник — клас слова, наприклад often. Обставина — роль слова або групи в реченні: at home складається з двох слів, але разом називає місце. Позицію обираємо за змістом і будовою, не за одним правилом для всіх прислівників.

metadata.prospective_learning_resource_descriptio: Порядок слів може виділяти хто, що, коли або де. Спочатку визначаємо фокус і зберігаємо всі факти; потім обираємо конструкцію. Не кожне підсилення є інверсією, і не всі такі моделі належать лише до офіційного письма.

prospective_page_metadata.description: Have got / has got називає те, що хтось має зараз: річ, родинний зв'язок, тварину чи ознаку.

metadata.prospective_learning_resource_descriptio: Have got / has got називає те, що хтось має зараз: річ, родинний зв'язок, тварину чи ознаку. Сестра — це родинний зв'язок, а не предмет власності. Основні приклади тут подано повними формами; скорочення також можуть бути правильними.
